meta.title: Quantum Mechanics I — Module I: The Wave Function
meta.subject: Quantum Mechanics I (MAT/PHY, Sem 5)

glossary.definition: A quantum state is the complete description of how a physical system is prepared, used to predict the probabilities of all measurement outcomes.
glossary.example: A particle prepared in state \(\Psi(x, t)\) inside a laboratory bottle.

glossary.definition: A conservative system is a physical system in which the force can be written as the negative spatial derivative of a potential energy function, \(F = -\partial V/\partial x\).
glossary.example: An electron moving in an electrostatic potential \(V(x)\).

glossary.definition: The complex conjugate of a complex number or function \(\Psi\), written \(\Psi^*\), is formed by reversing the sign of \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) everywhere it appears.
glossary.example: If \(\Psi = A e^{-i\omega t}\), then \(\Psi^* = A^* e^{+i\omega t}\).

glossary.definition: The wave function \(\Psi(x, t)\) is a complex-valued function of position \(x\) and time \(t\) that encodes the complete quantum state of a particle.
glossary.example: Solving Equation (1.1) with initial condition \(\Psi(x, 0)\) gives \(\Psi(x, t)\) for all future times.

glossary.definition: The Schrödinger equation is the fundamental partial differential equation of quantum mechanics that governs how the wave function \(\Psi(x, t)\) evolves in time.
glossary.example: Equation (1.1): \(i\hbar\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial t} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2\Psi}{\partial x^2} + V\Psi\).

glossary.definition: Planck's constant \(h\) is the fundamental action constant of quantum mechanics, usually written in reduced form as \(\hbar = h/(2\pi) = 1.054573 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J s}\).
glossary.example: Equation (1.2) defines \(\hbar\) as \(h\) divided by \(2\pi\).

glossary.definition: Born's statistical interpretation states that \(|\Psi(x, t)|^2\,dx\) is the probability of finding the particle between \(x\) and \(x + dx\) at time \(t\).
glossary.example: In Equation (1.3), the area under \(|\Psi(x, t)|^2\) from \(a\) to \(b\) gives the probability of finding the particle in that interval.

glossary.definition: Quantum indeterminacy is the principle that even when the wave function \(\Psi(x, t)\) is completely known, the exact outcome of an individual measurement cannot be predicted with certainty.
glossary.example: Before measurement, quantum theory gives only probabilities for where an electron will land on a screen.

glossary.definition: The realist position is the view advocated by Einstein that a particle already had a definite position before measurement, making quantum mechanics an incomplete theory.
glossary.example: If a detector finds the particle at \(C\), the realist says the particle was already at \(C\) just before the measurement.

glossary.definition: A hidden variable is hypothetical extra information beyond the wave function \(\Psi\) needed in a realist theory to specify a particle's exact properties prior to measurement.
glossary.example: Einstein argued that \(\Psi\) is not the whole story and must be supplemented by hidden variables.

glossary.definition: The Copenhagen (or orthodox) interpretation is the view associated with Bohr that a particle has no definite position before measurement, and the measurement itself compels it to take a definite value.
glossary.example: Bell's theorem and subsequent experiments confirmed the orthodox view over local hidden variables.

glossary.definition: The agnostic position is the stance that refuses to answer where a particle was before measurement because any test requires making a measurement first.
glossary.example: John Bell showed in 1964 that whether a particle had a definite prior position makes an observable experimental difference, ruling out agnosticism.

glossary.definition: Wave function collapse is the sudden, discontinuous change of \(\Psi(x, t)\) during a measurement into a sharp spike centered at the measured value.
glossary.example: Measuring the particle at point \(C\) collapses \(|\Psi|^2\) to a sharp peak at \(C\), so an immediate second measurement returns \(C\) again.

glossary.definition: Interference is the superposition of waves in which in-phase waves add constructively to form bright fringes and out-of-phase waves cancel destructively to form dark fringes.
glossary.example: In Example 1.1, single electrons sent through two slits accumulate into a two-slit interference pattern.

glossary.definition: A discrete variable is a variable that can take only isolated values, where the probability of outcome \(j\) is \(P(j) = N(j)/N\).
glossary.example: In Section 1.3.1, the integer age \(j\) in years of a person chosen from a room of \(N = 14\) people.

glossary.definition: The most probable value of a variable is the outcome \(j\) that has the highest probability \(P(j)\) (or highest peak of \(\rho(x)\)).
glossary.example: In the room of 14 people in Section 1.3.1, age 25 is the most probable value because five people share that age.

glossary.definition: The median is the value of a variable for which the probability of obtaining a larger result equals the probability of obtaining a smaller result.
glossary.example: In Section 1.3.1, the median age is 23 because 7 people are younger than 23 and 7 are older.

glossary.definition: The expectation value \(\langle j\rangle\) or \(\langle x\rangle\) is the weighted average of a quantity over all possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities.
glossary.example: In Equation (1.7), \(\langle j\rangle = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} jP(j)\); in Equation (1.28), \(\langle x\rangle = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} x|\Psi(x, t)|^2\,dx\).

glossary.definition: The variance \(\sigma^2\) of a distribution is the expectation value of the squared deviation from the average: \(\sigma^2 \equiv \langle(\Delta j)^2\rangle = \langle j^2\rangle - \langle j\rangle^2\).
glossary.example: Squaring \(\Delta j = j - \langle j\rangle\) before averaging prevents positive and negative deviations from canceling.

glossary.definition: The standard deviation \(\sigma = \sqrt{\langle j^2\rangle - \langle j\rangle^2}\) is the square root of the variance and measures the spread of a distribution about its expectation value.
glossary.example: A distribution with zero spread has \(\sigma = 0\) and \(\langle j^2\rangle = \langle j\rangle^2\).

glossary.definition: The probability density \(\rho(x)\) for a continuous variable is the probability per unit length, so that \(\rho(x)\,dx\) is the probability of landing between \(x\) and \(x + dx\).
glossary.example: In Equation (1.15), the probability of finding \(x\) between \(a\) and \(b\) is \(P_{ab} = \int_a^b \rho(x)\,dx\).

glossary.definition: A gaussian distribution is a symmetric bell-shaped continuous probability density of the form \(\rho(x) = A e^{-\lambda(x-a)^2}\) centered at \(x = a\).
glossary.example: For \(\rho(x) = A e^{-\lambda(x-a)^2}\), normalization gives \(A = \sqrt{\lambda/\pi}\) and expectation value \(\langle x\rangle = a\).

glossary.definition: Normalizing a wave function is the process of choosing its complex multiplicative constant \(A\) so that the total probability over all space equals 1: \(\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} |\Psi(x, t)|^2\,dx = 1\).
glossary.example: Equation (1.20) fixes the modulus \(|A|\) of the wave function while leaving its overall phase undetermined.

glossary.definition: A square-integrable function is a wave function \(\Psi(x, t)\) for which the integral of \(|\Psi(x, t)|^2\) over all space is finite and non-zero, so it can be normalized.
glossary.example: Physically realizable quantum states correspond to square-integrable solutions of the Schrödinger equation.

glossary.definition: A non-normalizable function is a solution to the Schrödinger equation whose integral \(\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} |\Psi|^2\,dx\) is infinite or zero, so it cannot represent a physical particle.
glossary.example: The trivial solution \(\Psi = 0\) and functions that do not vanish as \(|x| \to \infty\) are non-normalizable.

glossary.definition: An ensemble is a large collection of independent systems all prepared in the exact same quantum state \(\Psi\), used to define and measure expectation values.
glossary.example: Measuring position once on each bottle in a long row of identically prepared bottles yields the average \(\langle x\rangle\).

glossary.definition: An operator is a mathematical instruction that acts on the function following it to produce another function, used between \(\Psi^*\) and \(\Psi\) to compute expectation values.
glossary.example: In Equation (1.36), \(\langle Q(x, p)\rangle = \int \Psi^* [Q(x, -i\hbar\partial/\partial x)]\Psi\,dx\).

glossary.definition: In quantum mechanics on a line, momentum \(p\) is represented by the differential operator \(-i\hbar(\partial/\partial x)\) acting on the wave function \(\Psi(x, t)\).
glossary.example: Equation (1.33) gives \(\langle p\rangle = -i\hbar \int \Psi^*(\partial\Psi/\partial x)\,dx\).

glossary.definition: Ehrenfest's theorem is the principle that quantum expectation values obey relations analogous to classical mechanics, such as \(d\langle p\rangle/dt = \langle -\partial V/\partial x\rangle\).
glossary.example: Equation (1.32) \(\langle p\rangle = m\,d\langle x\rangle/dt\) and Equation (1.38) \(d\langle p\rangle/dt = \langle -\partial V/\partial x\rangle\) form Ehrenfest's theorem.

glossary.definition: The de Broglie formula \(p = h/\lambda = 2\pi\hbar/\lambda\) relates the momentum \(p\) of a quantum particle inversely to the wavelength \(\lambda\) of its wave function.
glossary.example: By Equation (1.39), a wave function with a single sharp wavelength \(\lambda\) has a single definite momentum \(p\).

glossary.definition: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states that the product of the standard deviation in position \(\sigma_x\) and the standard deviation in momentum \(\sigma_p\) is at least \(\hbar/2\).
glossary.example: Equation (1.40): \(\sigma_x\sigma_p \ge \hbar/2\), meaning a state sharply localized in position must have a wide spread in momentum.

cards.title: From a classical point path to a spread-out wave
cards.meaning: Instead of tracking a single point x(t), quantum mechanics describes a particle by a wave function spread along the x axis.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="18" y1="56" x2="242" y2="56" class="ik"/><rect x="130" y="36" width="34" height="16" class="s ok"/><circle cx="138" cy="54" r="3" class="f"/><circle cx="156" cy="54" r="3" class="f"/><line x1="164" y1="44" x2="202" y2="44" class="lk"/><text x="24" y="28" class="t">Classical: point x(t), force F(x,t)</text><text x="210" y="48" class="t">F(x,t)</text><line x1="18" y1="148" x2="242" y2="148" class="ik"/><path d="M 22 148 Q 52 146 72 132 Q 95 112 125 88 Q 145 72 165 110 Q 185 142 236 148" class="lk"/><text x="24" y="92" class="t">Quantum: wave function Ψ(x,t)</text><text x="236" y="164" class="t">x</text></svg>
cards.picture: Compare the classical cart at one position x(t) on top with the spread-out wave function Ψ(x,t) below.
cards.example: In classical mechanics Newton's law finds x(t); in quantum mechanics the Schrödinger equation finds Ψ(x,t).
cards.bridge: Given the initial wave function Ψ(x,0), the Schrödinger equation determines Ψ(x,t) for all future time.

cards.title: What is the Schrödinger equation?
cards.body: The wave function \(\Psi(x,t)\) describes the quantum state of a mass \(m\) in potential \(V\) and evolves by the Schrödinger equation, Equation (1.1).

cards.title: How a spread-out wave predicts where a point particle is found
cards.meaning: Born's statistical interpretation says the area under |Ψ(x,t)|² between a and b is the probability of finding the particle in that interval.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="78,142 78,108 92,86 106,62 114,52 114,142" class="s"/><line x1="18" y1="142" x2="244" y2="142" class="ik"/><line x1="62" y1="156" x2="62" y2="20" class="ik"/><path d="M 22 138 Q 48 112 68 122 Q 86 130 108 58 Q 124 22 142 76 Q 162 136 184 126 Q 208 114 238 138" class="lk"/><line x1="78" y1="142" x2="78" y2="108" class="gk"/><line x1="114" y1="142" x2="114" y2="52" class="gk"/><text x="76" y="30" class="t">|Ψ|²</text><text x="78" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">a</text><text x="114" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">b</text><text x="128" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">A</text><text x="168" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">B</text><text x="194" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">C</text><text x="240" y="158" class="t">x</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Figure 1.2: the shaded region between a and b gives the probability of finding the particle in [a, b].
cards.example: You are likely to find the particle near A where |Ψ|² is tall, and unlikely near B where |Ψ|² is low.
cards.bridge: Integrating |Ψ(x,t)|² = Ψ*Ψ from x = a to x = b gives Equation (1.3).

cards.title: What is Born's statistical interpretation?
cards.body: Born's statistical interpretation says \(|\Psi(x,t)|^2 = \Psi^*\Psi\) is the probability density, so integrating from \(a\) to \(b\) gives the probability in \([a,b]\).
cards.tex: \int_a^b |\Psi(x, t)|^2\,dx = \text{probability of finding the particle between } a \text{ and } b\text{, at time } t

cards.title: What are the realist, orthodox, and agnostic views?
cards.body: Before measurement finds a particle at \(C\), realists say it was at \(C\) via a hidden variable, the orthodox (Copenhagen) view says measurement produced \(C\), and agnostics refuse to answer.

cards.title: What is wave function collapse?
cards.body: Wave function collapse is the sudden jump of \(\Psi(x,t)\) during a measurement into a sharp spike at the measured point \(C\), so an immediate repeat measurement gives \(C\) again.

cards.label: Example 1.1 · §1.2
cards.title: Example 1.1: Electron Interference
cards.legend: \(\Psi_1, \Psi_2\) waves from slit 1 and slit 2, \(|\Psi|^2\) landing probability density on the screen, \(I_{\text{int}}\) interference term.

phases.name: Two-slit wave
phases.why: each electron wave passes through both slits at once

phases.name: Born probability
phases.why: compute |Ψ|² = Ψ*Ψ for spots on the screen

phases.name: Interference fringes
phases.why: cross terms create bright and dark fringes over many electrons

phases.name: Slit detection
phases.why: measuring which slit collapses Ψ and destroys fringes

steps.note: With both slits open, one electron's wave function is the sum of waves from both slits.

ask.q: By Born's rule in Equation (1.3), what gives the screen spot probability density?
ask.why: According to Equation (1.3), the probability density of an electron landing at x is |Ψ(x,t)|² = Ψ*(x,t)Ψ(x,t).

steps.note: Each individual electron produces one dot at a random spot weighted by \(|\Psi(x, t)|^2\).
Substitute the two-slit superposition into \(\Psi^*\Psi\).

ask.q: What do we get when we expand the product \((\Psi_1^* + \Psi_2^*)(\Psi_1 + \Psi_2)\)?
ask.why: Multiplying the two brackets produces the two single-slit intensities plus two cross terms.

steps.note: The cross terms \(\Psi_1^*\Psi_2 + \Psi_2^*\Psi_1\) encode constructive and destructive interference.
Waiting for many single electrons builds up the two-slit fringe pattern dot by dot.

ask.q: In Example 1.1, why do single electrons still form an interference pattern?
ask.why: With both slits open and no measurement in flight, each electron's wave passes through both slits and interferes with itself.

steps.note: Closing slit 2 or detecting the electron at slit 1 collapses \(\Psi\) and erases the fringes.

ask.q: Why does detecting which slit each electron passes through destroy the interference fringes?
options: The electron loses all its mass
ask.why: Detecting the electron at one slit collapses the wave function to that slit alone, removing the second wave and the interference term.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Equation (1.3), what does the integral \(\int_a^b |\Psi(x,t)|^2\,dx\) represent?
options: Probability of finding particle in \([a, b]\)
cards.why: Born's statistical interpretation in Equation (1.3) states that the area under |Ψ(x,t)|² between a and b is the probability of finding the particle in that interval at time t.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: If a particle is measured at \(C\), what does the orthodox (Copenhagen) view say?
options: Measurement compelled it to take position \(C\)
It was already at \(C\) before measurement
A second measurement will never give \(C\)
cards.why: In the orthodox (Copenhagen) interpretation, the particle had no precise position prior to measurement; the act of measurement forced it to take the value C.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: When a measurement finds a particle at \(C\), the wave function suddenly ______ to a spike at \(C\).
cards.why: Upon measurement, the wave function collapses discontinuously to a sharp spike about C so an immediate second measurement returns the same value C.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Example 1.1, how does the pattern form when electrons arrive one at a time?
options: Individual spots accumulate into interference fringes
One electron draws the entire smooth pattern
Two smooth bands appear without any fringes
All electrons hit the exact same point
cards.why: Each electron lands as a single localized dot at a random position governed by |Ψ|², and over thousands of electrons the dots build up the two-slit interference fringes.

cards.title: Most probable, median, and average in a histogram
cards.meaning: A discrete distribution counts how many members N(j) have each value j, giving probabilities P(j) = N(j)/N.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="146" x2="244" y2="146" class="ik"/><line x1="28" y1="154" x2="28" y2="22" class="ik"/><rect x="48" y="128" width="16" height="18" class="s ok"/><rect x="64" y="128" width="16" height="18" class="s ok"/><rect x="80" y="92" width="16" height="54" class="s ok"/><rect x="148" y="110" width="16" height="36" class="s ok"/><rect x="180" y="110" width="16" height="36" class="s ok"/><rect x="196" y="56" width="16" height="90" class="f"/><line x1="138" y1="146" x2="138" y2="38" class="gk"/><text x="36" y="32" class="t">N(j)</text><text x="56" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="t">14</text><text x="88" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="t">16</text><text x="138" y="32" text-anchor="middle" class="t">⟨j⟩ = 21</text><text x="172" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="t">23</text><text x="204" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="t">25</text><text x="240" y="162" class="t">j</text></svg>
cards.picture: Look at Figure 1.5 for the 14 people: the tallest bar is at 25, the halfway split is at 23, and the balance point is ⟨j⟩ = 21.
cards.example: In Section 1.3.1, nobody has age 21 or 23, yet the average age is 21 and the median age is 23.
cards.bridge: Weighting each value j by its probability P(j) = N(j)/N defines the expectation value ⟨j⟩ in Equation (1.7).

cards.title: What are discrete probability, mode, and median?
cards.body: For a discrete variable with \(N = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} N(j)\), the probability of \(j\) is \(P(j) = N(j)/N\) with \(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} P(j) = 1\); the most probable \(j\) maximizes \(P(j)\) and the median splits probability equally.

cards.title: What is the expectation value of a discrete variable?
cards.body: The expectation value \(\langle j\rangle\) is the weighted average \(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} jP(j)\), and for any function \(f(j)\) it is \(\langle f(j)\rangle = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} f(j)P(j)\).

cards.title: What are variance and standard deviation?
cards.body: The variance \(\sigma^2 \equiv \langle(\Delta j)^2\rangle\) is the average squared deviation from \(\langle j\rangle\), and its square root \(\sigma = \sqrt{\langle j^2\rangle - \langle j\rangle^2}\) is the standard deviation measuring spread.
cards.tex: \Delta j = j - \langle j\rangle, \quad \sigma^2 \equiv \langle (\Delta j)^2\rangle, \quad \sigma = \sqrt{\langle j^2\rangle - \langle j\rangle^2}, \quad \langle j^2\rangle \ge \langle j\rangle^2

cards.label: Derivation · §1.3.1
cards.title: Variance theorem and Equation (1.12), step by step
cards.legend: \(\Delta j = j - \langle j\rangle\) deviation from average, \(P(j)\) probability of \(j\), \(\sigma^2\) variance, \(\sigma\) standard deviation.

phases.name: Definition
phases.why: write variance as the average of (j - <j>)²

phases.name: Expand square
phases.why: multiply out (j - <j>)² inside the sum

phases.name: Identify averages
phases.why: use Equations (1.6), (1.7), and (1.8)

phases.name: Standard deviation
phases.why: combine terms and take the square root

steps.note: Start from Equation (1.10) and Equation (1.11) for the variance \(\sigma^2 = \langle(\Delta j)^2\rangle\).

ask.q: Why do we square \(\Delta j = j - \langle j\rangle\) before averaging?
options: To make the median equal zero
ask.why: Positive and negative deviations cancel so ⟨Δj⟩ = ⟨j⟩ − ⟨j⟩ = 0; squaring makes every term non-negative.

steps.note: Expand \((j - \langle j\rangle)^2 = j^2 - 2j\langle j\rangle + \langle j\rangle^2\).

ask.q: Since \(\langle j\rangle\) is a constant number, how does the sum split?
ask.why: Because ⟨j⟩ does not depend on the summation index j, both 2⟨j⟩ and ⟨j⟩² can be factored outside the sums.

steps.tex: \sigma^2 = \sum j^2 P(j) - 2\langle j\rangle \sum j P(j) + \langle j\rangle^2 \sum P(j)
steps.note: Separate the three sums and pull the constant \(\langle j\rangle\) outside.

ask.q: What are the values of \(\sum j^2P(j)\), \(\sum jP(j)\), and \(\sum P(j)\)?
ask.why: By Equations (1.8), (1.7), and (1.6), the three sums equal ⟨j²⟩, ⟨j⟩, and 1 respectively.

steps.note: Replace each sum using Equations (1.8), (1.7), and (1.6).
Combine \(-2\langle j\rangle^2 + \langle j\rangle^2 = -\langle j\rangle^2\).

ask.q: How do we obtain the standard deviation \(\sigma\) in Equation (1.12)?
ask.why: The standard deviation σ is the square root of the variance σ², yielding Equation (1.12).

steps.note: Taking the square root gives Equation (1.12), and \(\sigma^2 \ge 0\) implies \(\langle j^2\rangle \ge \langle j\rangle^2\).

cards.title: Why continuous variables use probability density ρ(x)
cards.meaning: For a continuous variable x, the chance of hitting one exact real number is zero, so we measure the probability ρ(x)dx of landing in a tiny interval dx.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="112,142 112,56 126,62 126,142" class="f"/><polygon points="76,142 76,84 94,62 112,56 126,62 146,82 162,102 162,142" class="s"/><line x1="18" y1="142" x2="242" y2="142" class="ik"/><line x1="42" y1="156" x2="42" y2="20" class="ik"/><path d="M 22 140 Q 56 132 76 84 Q 104 34 134 70 Q 168 112 234 140" class="lk"/><text x="56" y="30" class="t">ρ(x)</text><text x="76" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">a</text><text x="119" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">dx</text><text x="162" y="158" text-anchor="middle" class="t">b</text><text x="186" y="52" class="t">Strip area = ρ(x)dx</text><text x="238" y="158" class="t">x</text></svg>
cards.picture: A thin strip of width dx has area ρ(x)dx; adding all strips from a to b gives the integral P_ab.
cards.example: The chance a person's age lies in a two-day window is twice the chance for a one-day window.
cards.bridge: Sums over discrete j become integrals over continuous x in Equations (1.15) to (1.19).

cards.title: What is probability density for continuous variables?
cards.body: The probability density \(\rho(x)\) gives the probability \(\rho(x)\,dx\) in \([x, x+dx]\), so \(P_{ab} = \int_a^b \rho(x)\,dx\), \(\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\rho(x)\,dx = 1\), and \(\langle f(x)\rangle = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f(x)\rho(x)\,dx\).

cards.label: Example 1.2 · §1.3.2
cards.title: Example 1.2: Falling rock probability density and ⟨x⟩
cards.legend: \(h\) cliff height, \(x(t)\) distance fallen at time \(t\), \(T = \sqrt{2h/g}\) total flight time, \(\rho(x)\) probability density.

phases.name: Kinematics
phases.why: relate distance fallen x(t) to speed dx/dt

phases.name: Time fraction
phases.why: equate snapshot probability ρ(x)dx to dt/T

phases.name: Probability density
phases.why: simplify to find ρ(x) on 0 ≤ x ≤ h

phases.name: Average distance
phases.why: integrate xρ(x) from 0 to h using Equation (1.17)

steps.note: A rock dropped from rest falls distance \(x(t) = \frac{1}{2}gt^2\) in time \(t\), with total flight time \(T = \sqrt{2h/g}\).
Differentiate \(x(t)\) with respect to \(t\) to find the downward velocity.

ask.q: In Example 1.2, what is the probability of a random snapshot occurring in \([t, t+dt]\)?
ask.why: Since photographs are snapped at random times over the total flight duration T, the probability of landing in interval dt is dt/T.

steps.note: Set the distance probability \(\rho(x)\,dx\) equal to the time fraction \(dt/T\).
Substitute \(dt = dx/(gt)\) and \(T = \sqrt{2h/g}\).

ask.q: Using \(gt = \sqrt{2gx}\), what does \(\frac{dx}{gt}\sqrt{\frac{g}{2h}}\) simplify to?
ask.why: Replacing gt by √(2gx) cancels √g and gives dx / (2√(hx)).

steps.note: This is the probability density for \(0 \le x \le h\) (Figure 1.7), whose integral from \(0\) to \(h\) equals \(1\).

ask.q: Which integral gives the average distance \(\langle x\rangle\) by Equation (1.17)?
ask.why: By Equation (1.17), the expectation value of x is the integral of xρ(x) over the allowed range 0 to h.

steps.note: Substitute \(\rho(x)\) into Equation (1.17) and simplify \(x/\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}\).

ask.q: What is the antiderivative of \(x^{1/2}\) with respect to \(x\)?
ask.why: By the power rule, ∫ x^{1/2} dx = (2/3)x^{3/2}.

steps.note: Evaluate the antiderivative \(\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\) from \(0\) to \(h\).
The average distance fallen is \(h/3\), which is less than \(h/2\) because the rock moves slowly near the top.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: In Section 1.3.1, what is the average age \(\langle j\rangle\) of the 14 people in the room?
cards.why: Adding all 14 ages gives 14 + 15 + 3(16) + 2(22) + 2(24) + 5(25) = 294, and dividing by 14 gives ⟨j⟩ = 21 years.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: A room has two babies aged 1 and 3 years. What is the standard deviation \(\sigma\)?
cards.why: Here ⟨j⟩ = 2 so ⟨j⟩² = 4, and ⟨j²⟩ = (1² + 3²)/2 = 5. By Equation (1.12), σ = √(5 − 4) = 1 year.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Example 1.2, why is the average distance \(\langle x\rangle = h/3\) less than \(h/2\)?
options: The rock spends more time near the top
Gravity weakens as the rock falls
Air resistance stops the rock at \(h/3\)
cards.why: Starting from rest, the rock moves slowly near x = 0 and speeds up as it falls, so random time snapshots catch it near the top more often.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: For a continuous variable \(x\), the function \(\rho(x)\) in Equation (1.14) is called the probability ______.
cards.why: Because ρ(x)dx is a probability and dx has units of length, ρ(x) is probability per unit length, called the probability density.

cards.title: Scaling a wave function so total probability equals 1
cards.meaning: Because the particle must be somewhere on the x axis, the total area under |Ψ(x,t)|² from −∞ to +∞ must equal 1.
cards.picture: Multiplying Ψ by a constant A scales the height of |Ψ|² until the shaded area over all x equals 1.
cards.example: If ∫|Ψ|²dx = 4, multiplying Ψ by A = 1/2 divides the area by |A|² = 1/4 so the new area is 1.
cards.bridge: Because Equation (1.1) is linear in Ψ, AΨ(x,t) is also a solution, allowing us to enforce Equation (1.20).

cards.title: What is normalizing a wave function?
cards.body: Normalizing a wave function means choosing its multiplicative constant \(A\) so that the integral of \(|\Psi(x,t)|^2\) over all space equals \(1\), as required by Equation (1.20).

cards.title: What are square-integrable and non-normalizable states?
cards.body: Square-integrable functions have a finite non-zero integral \(\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}|\Psi|^2\,dx\) and represent physical states, whereas non-normalizable solutions (infinite integral or \(\Psi=0\)) are rejected.

cards.label: Derivation · §1.4
cards.title: Conservation of normalization (Equations (1.21)–(1.27))
cards.legend: \(\Psi(x,t)\) wave function, \(\Psi^*(x,t)\) complex conjugate, \(V(x)\) real potential energy, \(m\) particle mass.

phases.name: Differentiate integral
phases.why: bring d/dt inside the spatial integral as ∂/∂t

phases.name: Use Schrödinger equation
phases.why: substitute ∂Ψ/∂t and ∂Ψ*/∂t from Equations (1.23) and (1.24)

phases.name: Exact x-derivative
phases.why: rewrite ∂|Ψ|²/∂t as ∂/∂x of a bracket in Equation (1.25)

phases.name: Boundary evaluation
phases.why: integrate over x and use Ψ(±∞,t) = 0 to get Equation (1.27)

steps.note: Start with Equation (1.21): total derivative \(d/dt\) outside becomes \(\partial/\partial t\) inside.

ask.q: By the product rule on \(|\Psi|^2 = \Psi^*\Psi\), what is \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}|\Psi|^2\)?
ask.why: Since |Ψ|² = Ψ*Ψ is a product of two time-dependent functions, the product rule gives Equation (1.22).

steps.note: Apply the product rule to \(\Psi^*\Psi\) to get Equation (1.22).

ask.q: When we substitute Equations (1.23) and (1.24), what happens to the \(V\Psi^*\Psi\) terms?
ask.why: Because V is real, −(i/ħ)VΨ*Ψ from ∂Ψ/∂t and +(i/ħ)VΨ*Ψ from ∂Ψ*/∂t cancel completely.

steps.note: Substitute Equations (1.23) and (1.24); the potential terms \(\mp(i/\hbar)V\Psi^*\Psi\) cancel.
Write the right side as an exact \(x\)-derivative (Equation (1.25)), since \(\frac{\partial\Psi^*}{\partial x}\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial x}\) cancels.

ask.q: How do we evaluate \(\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}[\cdots]\,dx\) in Equation (1.26)?
ask.why: By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the integral of ∂F/∂x from −∞ to +∞ is simply F(+∞) − F(−∞).

steps.note: Integrating Equation (1.25) with respect to \(x\) gives the boundary expression in Equation (1.26).

ask.q: Why does the boundary term at \(x = \pm\infty\) equal zero?
ask.why: A square-integrable wave function and its spatial derivatives must vanish as x → ±∞.

steps.note: Equation (1.27): the integral is constant in time, so if \(\Psi\) is normalized at \(t=0\), it stays normalized forever.

cards.label: Worked Derivation · §1.4
cards.title: Normalizing Ψ(x,t) = Ae^{-λ|x|}e^{-iωt} (Section 1.4)

phases.name: Modulus squared
phases.why: find |Ψ(x,t)|² = Ψ*Ψ and cancel the time phase

phases.name: Normalization integral
phases.why: set the integral over (−∞, +∞) equal to 1 and use symmetry

phases.name: Integrate
phases.why: evaluate the exponential integral on [0, ∞)

phases.name: Solve for A
phases.why: isolate the positive constant A

steps.note: Since \(e^{+i\omega t}e^{-i\omega t} = 1\) and \(A\) is positive real, \(|\Psi(x,t)|^2 = A^2 e^{-2\lambda|x|}\).

ask.q: What condition must \(|\Psi(x,t)|^2\) satisfy by Equation (1.20)?
ask.why: Normalization (Equation (1.20)) requires that the integral of |Ψ(x,t)|² from −∞ to +∞ equals 1.

steps.note: Substitute \(|\Psi(x,t)|^2\) into the normalization condition Equation (1.20).

ask.q: Because \(e^{-2\lambda|x|}\) is an even function of \(x\), how can we simplify the integral?
options: Set the integral equal to zero
ask.why: For any even integrand, the integral from −∞ to +∞ is twice the integral from 0 to +∞, where |x| = x.

steps.note: Use even symmetry to write twice the integral over \(0 \le x < \infty\), where \(|x| = x\).

ask.q: What is the value of \(\int_0^{+\infty} e^{-2\lambda x}\,dx\) for \(\lambda > 0\)?
ask.why: The antiderivative is −e^{−2λx}/(2λ), which evaluates to 0 − (−1/(2λ)) = 1/(2λ).

steps.note: Evaluating \(2A^2 \left(\frac{1}{2\lambda}\right) = 1\) cancels the factor of \(2\).
Multiply both sides by \(\lambda\).

ask.q: Given that \(A\) is a positive real constant, what is \(A\)?
ask.why: Taking the positive square root of A² = λ gives A = √λ.

steps.note: Taking the positive square root gives the normalized constant \(A = \sqrt{\lambda}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Which solution to the Schrödinger equation can represent a physically realizable particle?
options: A wave function with infinite integral
cards.why: Only square-integrable solutions—those with a finite, non-zero integral of |Ψ|² over all space—can be normalized to satisfy Equation (1.20).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Why must we not keep renormalizing \(\Psi(x,t)\) with a time-dependent factor \(A(t)\)?
cards.why: If A were a function of t, the time derivative ∂/∂t in Equation (1.1) would pick up an extra (dA/dt)Ψ term, so A(t)Ψ would no longer solve the Schrödinger equation.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What property of a complex normalization factor \(A\) is left undetermined by Equation (1.20)?
cards.why: Normalization fixes only the modulus |A| because |e^{iθ}|² = 1; the complex phase of A remains undetermined and carries no physical significance.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Physically realizable quantum states correspond to ______-integrable solutions of the Schrödinger equation.
cards.why: A wave function is normalizable if and only if the integral of its modulus squared |Ψ|² is finite and non-zero, i.e., it is square-integrable.

cards.title: Why ⟨x⟩ is measured on a shelf of identical bottles
cards.meaning: An expectation value is the average of single measurements made on a large ensemble of identically prepared systems, not repeated measurements on one particle.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="16" y1="122" x2="244" y2="122" class="ik"/><rect x="28" y="64" width="52" height="58" class="s ok"/><rect x="104" y="64" width="52" height="58" class="s ok"/><rect x="180" y="64" width="52" height="58" class="s ok"/><path d="M 34 114 Q 54 72 74 114" class="lk"/><path d="M 110 114 Q 130 72 150 114" class="lk"/><path d="M 186 114 Q 206 72 226 114" class="lk"/><circle cx="48" cy="104" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="138" cy="104" r="3.5" class="f"/><circle cx="204" cy="104" r="3.5" class="f"/><text x="54" y="52" text-anchor="middle" class="t">State Ψ</text><text x="130" y="52" text-anchor="middle" class="t">State Ψ</text><text x="206" y="52" text-anchor="middle" class="t">State Ψ</text><text x="130" y="152" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Ensemble average = ⟨x⟩</text></svg>
cards.picture: Picture a row of bottles on a shelf, each holding a particle prepared in the same state Ψ, measured all at once.
cards.example: Measuring one particle repeatedly just repeats the first collapsed value C; measuring 1000 identical bottles gives ⟨x⟩.
cards.bridge: Weighting every position x by the probability density |Ψ(x,t)|² gives Equation (1.28) for ⟨x⟩.

cards.title: What is a quantum ensemble and ⟨x⟩?
cards.body: An ensemble is a collection of identically prepared systems all in state \(\Psi\); the expectation value \(\langle x\rangle\) in Equation (1.28) is the average of position measurements across this ensemble.

cards.label: Derivation · §1.5
cards.title: Expectation value of momentum (Equations (1.29)–(1.33))
cards.legend: \(\langle x\rangle\) expectation value of position, \(\langle v\rangle = d\langle x\rangle/dt\) velocity expectation value, \(\langle p\rangle = m\langle v\rangle\) momentum expectation value.

phases.name: Differentiate <x>
phases.why: take d/dt of Equation (1.28) and substitute Equation (1.25)

phases.name: First integration by parts
phases.why: move ∂/∂x onto x to reach Equation (1.30)

phases.name: Second integration by parts
phases.why: move ∂/∂x off Ψ* onto Ψ to reach Equation (1.31)

phases.name: Momentum formula
phases.why: multiply by mass m using Equations (1.32) and (1.33)

steps.note: Differentiate Equation (1.28) with respect to time \(t\) (limits \(\pm\infty\) understood).

ask.q: Which identity replaces \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}|\Psi|^2\) to give Equation (1.29)?
ask.why: Substituting Equation (1.25) expresses ∂|Ψ|²/∂t as a spatial derivative ∂/∂x so we can integrate by parts.

steps.note: This is Equation (1.29), with \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\) acting on the bracket.

ask.q: When we integrate by parts to move \(\partial/\partial x\) onto \(x\), what changes?
options: Pick up a minus sign and \(\partial x/\partial x = 1\)
ask.why: Integration by parts peels ∂/∂x off the bracket onto x (giving ∂x/∂x = 1) with a minus sign, and the boundary term vanishes at ±∞.

steps.note: Equation (1.30): used \(\partial x/\partial x = 1\) and dropped the boundary term at \(\pm\infty\).

ask.q: What does a second integration by parts on \(-\int \frac{\partial\Psi^*}{\partial x}\Psi\,dx\) give?
ask.why: Moving ∂/∂x from Ψ* onto Ψ introduces another minus sign, turning −∫(∂Ψ*/∂x)Ψ dx into +∫Ψ*(∂Ψ/∂x) dx.

steps.note: Equation (1.31): the two identical terms \(\Psi^*\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial x}\) add together, canceling the \(2\).

ask.q: Using \(\langle v\rangle = d\langle x\rangle/dt\) in Equation (1.32), how do we get \(\langle p\rangle\)?
ask.why: Since momentum is p = mv, Equation (1.33) defines ⟨p⟩ = m(d⟨x⟩/dt), which cancels 1/m.

steps.note: Equation (1.33): multiplying by \(m\) gives the expectation value of momentum directly from \(\Psi\).

cards.title: Sandwiching an operator between Ψ* and Ψ
cards.meaning: An operator is an instruction to do something to the function that follows it, such as multiplying by x or differentiating with respect to x.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="24" y="62" width="54" height="48" class="s ok"/><rect x="92" y="54" width="76" height="64" class="f"/><rect x="182" y="62" width="54" height="48" class="s ok"/><line x1="78" y1="86" x2="92" y2="86" class="ik"/><line x1="168" y1="86" x2="182" y2="86" class="ik"/><text x="51" y="90" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Ψ*</text><text x="130" y="82" text-anchor="middle" class="i">Operator</text><text x="130" y="100" text-anchor="middle" class="i">Q(x, -iħ∂/∂x)</text><text x="209" y="90" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Ψ</text><text x="130" y="34" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Sandwich inside ∫ ... dx</text><text x="130" y="148" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Output: expectation value ⟨Q⟩</text></svg>
cards.picture: To find any expectation value ⟨Q⟩, sandwich the operator for Q between Ψ* on the left and Ψ on the right, then integrate.
cards.example: The position operator [x] multiplies Ψ by x; the momentum operator [−iħ∂/∂x] differentiates Ψ and multiplies by −iħ.
cards.bridge: Replacing every p in a classical variable Q(x,p) by −iħ(∂/∂x) gives Equation (1.36).

cards.title: What are the position and momentum operators?
cards.body: An operator is an instruction acting on the function that follows: the operator \(x\) represents position and the operator \(-i\hbar(\partial/\partial x)\) represents momentum, sandwiched between \(\Psi^*\) and \(\Psi\).

cards.title: Expectation value of any dynamical variable Q(x,p)
cards.body: For any classical dynamical variable \(Q(x,p)\), replace every \(p\) by \(-i\hbar(\partial/\partial x)\), sandwich the operator between \(\Psi^*\) and \(\Psi\), and integrate (Equations (1.36) and (1.37)).

cards.title: What is Ehrenfest's theorem?
cards.body: Ehrenfest's theorem states that quantum expectation values obey classical laws, such as \(\langle p\rangle = m\,d\langle x\rangle/dt\) and Equation (1.38) \(d\langle p\rangle/dt = \langle -\partial V/\partial x\rangle\).
cards.tex: \frac{d\langle p\rangle}{dt} = \left\langle -\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\right\rangle, \qquad \langle p\rangle = m\frac{d\langle x\rangle}{dt}

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Equation (1.35), which operator represents momentum \(p\) in position space?
cards.why: By Equation (1.35), the momentum operator is −iħ(∂/∂x), which differentiates the wave function with respect to x and multiplies by −iħ.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: By Equation (1.37), which expression gives the expectation value of kinetic energy \(\langle T\rangle\)?
cards.why: Since T = p²/(2m), replacing p by −iħ(∂/∂x) twice gives the operator −(ħ²/2m)(∂²/∂x²), yielding Equation (1.37).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: The expectation value \(\langle x\rangle\) is the average of measurements on an ______ of identically prepared systems.
cards.why: Repeatedly measuring one particle just repeats the collapsed value; ⟨x⟩ is the average across an ensemble of identically prepared systems all in state Ψ.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What does Ehrenfest's theorem in Equation (1.38) state?
cards.why: Equation (1.38) states that d⟨p⟩/dt = ⟨−∂V/∂x⟩, which is the quantum expectation-value analog of Newton's second law F = dp/dt.

cards.title: Why a wave on a rope cannot have both a sharp position and a sharp wavelength
cards.meaning: A long regular wave has a clear wavelength λ but is spread out in position x, whereas a narrow bump has a clear position x but no well-defined wavelength λ.
cards.picture: Compare Figure 1.8 (many cycles, clear wavelength λ) with Figure 1.9 (one narrow bump, clear position x).
cards.example: Shaking a rope rhythmically makes a wave spread over 50 feet with λ ≈ 6 feet; one sudden jerk makes a narrow bump with no clear λ.
cards.bridge: Because the de Broglie formula p = h/λ = 2πħ/λ links wavelength to momentum, position spread and momentum spread trade off.

cards.title: What is the de Broglie formula?
cards.body: The de Broglie formula in Equation (1.39) states that the momentum \(p\) of a particle is inversely proportional to the wavelength \(\lambda\) of its wave function: \(p = h/\lambda = 2\pi\hbar/\lambda\).
examples: Spread in λ → spread in p

cards.title: The trade-off between position spread σ_x and momentum spread σ_p
cards.meaning: Squeezing the position spread σ_x of a quantum state forces its momentum spread σ_p to grow so that their product stays at least ħ/2.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="52,24 56,56 68,88 92,114 132,130 188,138 236,142 236,24" class="s"/><line x1="36" y1="148" x2="242" y2="148" class="ik"/><line x1="36" y1="148" x2="36" y2="20" class="ik"/><path d="M 52 24 Q 60 104 108 124 Q 156 140 236 142" class="lk"/><circle cx="86" cy="110" r="4" class="f"/><text x="152" y="68" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Allowed: σ_x σ_p ≥ ħ/2</text><text x="128" y="114" class="t">Gaussian: ħ/2</text><text x="56" y="32" class="t">σ_p</text><text x="232" y="164" class="t">σ_x</text></svg>
cards.picture: Every physical state lies on or above the boundary curve σ_x σ_p = ħ/2 in the (σ_x, σ_p) plane.
cards.example: A narrow spike has small σ_x and large σ_p; a long sine wave has small σ_p and large σ_x.
cards.bridge: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle in Equation (1.40) states this lower bound quantitatively as σ_x σ_p ≥ ħ/2.

cards.title: What is Heisenberg's uncertainty principle?
cards.body: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle in Equation (1.40) states that the product of the standard deviation in position \(\sigma_x\) and the standard deviation in momentum \(\sigma_p\) is at least \(\hbar/2\).

cards.title: What do σ_x and σ_p mean in measurements?
cards.body: Individual position or momentum measurements still yield precise numbers; \(\sigma_x\) and \(\sigma_p\) measure the spread of outcomes across an ensemble of identically prepared systems.

cards.label: Worked Derivation · §1.6
cards.title: Uncertainty product for a Gaussian wave packet (Section 1.6)
cards.legend: \(\Psi(x,t) = Ae^{-a[(mx^2/\hbar)+it]}\), \(A, a, m\) positive constants, \(\sigma_x\) position spread, \(\sigma_p\) momentum spread.

phases.name: Probability density
phases.why: take |Ψ(x,t)|² for the Gaussian wave function

phases.name: Normalize
phases.why: use Equation (1.20) to determine |A|²

phases.name: Position spread
phases.why: compute σ_x from ⟨x²⟩ and ⟨x⟩ = 0

phases.name: Momentum & product
phases.why: compute σ_p and verify σ_x σ_p = ħ/2

steps.note: For \(\Psi(x,t) = Ae^{-a[(mx^2/\hbar)+it]}\), the time factor \(|e^{-iat}|^2 = 1\) drops out.

ask.q: Using \(\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-2amx^2/\hbar}\,dx = \sqrt{\frac{\pi\hbar}{2am}}\), what does normalization give for \(|A|^2\)?
ask.why: Setting |A|² times the Gaussian integral √(πħ/(2am)) equal to 1 gives |A|² = √(2am/(πħ)).

steps.note: Equation (1.20) fixes the normalization factor \(|A|^2 = \sqrt{2am/(\pi\hbar)}\).

ask.q: Since \(|\Psi|^2\) is even about \(x = 0\), what is \(\langle x\rangle\)?
ask.why: The integrand x|Ψ(x,t)|² is an odd function of x, so its integral from −∞ to +∞ is zero.

steps.note: With \(\langle x\rangle = 0\), the Gaussian integral for \(\langle x^2\rangle\) gives \(\sigma_x^2 = \langle x^2\rangle = \frac{\hbar}{4am}\).
Take the square root to get the position standard deviation \(\sigma_x\).

ask.q: With \(\langle p\rangle = 0\) and \(\langle p^2\rangle = am\hbar\), what is the momentum spread \(\sigma_p\)?
ask.why: By Equation (1.12) applied to p, σ_p = √(⟨p²⟩ − ⟨p⟩²) = √(amħ − 0) = √(amħ).

steps.note: From \(\langle p^2\rangle = -\hbar^2\int \Psi^*\frac{\partial^2\Psi}{\partial x^2}\,dx = am\hbar\) and \(\langle p\rangle = 0\), we get \(\sigma_p = \sqrt{am\hbar}\).

ask.q: What do we get when we multiply \(\sigma_x = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{4am}}\) and \(\sigma_p = \sqrt{am\hbar}\)?
ask.why: The factors of a and m cancel inside the square root, leaving √(ħ²/4) = ħ/2, which achieves the minimum in Equation (1.40).

steps.note: A Gaussian wave packet achieves the minimum uncertainty product \(\sigma_x\sigma_p = \hbar/2\) in Equation (1.40).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: According to the de Broglie formula in Equation (1.39), how is momentum \(p\) related to wavelength \(\lambda\)?
cards.why: Equation (1.39) states that p = h/λ = 2πħ/λ, so a shorter wavelength corresponds to a larger momentum.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is Heisenberg's uncertainty principle as stated in Equation (1.40)?
cards.why: Equation (1.40) states that the product of the standard deviations in position and momentum is always greater than or equal to ħ/2.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: For a minimum-uncertainty state with \(\sigma_x\sigma_p = \hbar/2\) and \(\sigma_x = 0.5\text{ nm}\), what is \(\sigma_p/\hbar\)?
cards.why: From σ_x σ_p = ħ/2, we have σ_p/ħ = 1/(2σ_x) = 1/(2 × 0.5 nm) = 1 nm⁻¹.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: A state shaped like a long sinusoidal wave has a well-defined ______ but widely scattered position measurements.
cards.why: A long sinusoidal wave has a well-defined wavelength λ and therefore a well-defined momentum p = 2πħ/λ, at the cost of a large spread in position x.
